title: Bookmark Import Audit
user: People moving a years-old browser bookmark library who need to preserve its nested meaning and find destructive import problems before committing to a new manager.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker has thousands of manually filed bookmarks that became difficult to manage and explicitly wants categorization and content search.
A Linkwarden user reports that HTML import merges same-named folders from different paths, destroying the original directory structure.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 reports, plus HN commenters describing abandonment of bookmarks once libraries grow; import damage is high-severity because it is hard to reconstruct.
current_workaround: Import blindly, hand-clean folders afterward, or keep an unusable browser-export HTML file as a backup.
incumbents_and_gap: Linkwarden, Raindrop, and browser managers organize links after import, but do not foreground a dry-run that proves folder-path collisions, duplicate URLs, redirects, and missing titles before mutation.
smallest_useful_product: A fully local web app that reads Netscape bookmark HTML, builds a path-aware inventory, flags lossy-import hazards and duplicate/redirect clusters, and exports a corrected HTML plus a review CSV. Non-goals: hosting bookmarks, crawling the web, or AI-written summaries.
success_measure: In a 20-library pilot, at least 70% of imports identify one actionable collision or duplicate cluster before users import into a destination manager.
monetization: one-time — the sensitive export stays in-browser and the utility has a discrete migration value.
constraints: Process bookmark files locally; never fetch private URLs by default; clearly preserve original files and use deterministic URL normalization.
why_distinct: It is an import safety inspection and repair tool, not another bookmark database or a thin categorization wrapper.

title: Photo Cull Review
user: Households with large photo archives who need to safely decide which duplicate, burst, and unwanted media can be removed before backup costs and browsing noise grow further.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An owner of 2 TB of photos/videos asks how to remove duplicates and unwanted media because backup cost and browsing noise are becoming untenable.
An Immich external-library scan incorrectly marked thousands of existing assets offline/deleted, illustrating why bulk media actions require an independently reviewable plan.

recurrence: Two separate archive-management reports; the HN request includes a concrete 2 TB library and an escalating storage cost, while a large-library incident shows the risk of trusting bulk operations.
current_workaround: Run a duplicate finder, delete in batches, or postpone cleanup because tools offer opaque matches and destructive actions.
incumbents_and_gap: czkawka, dupeGuru, Immich, and PhotoPrism find duplicates or host libraries; the gap is a local, reversible human review queue that explains why assets were grouped and emits a deletion plan rather than deleting.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop-local PWA that indexes selected folders, groups exact hashes and visually similar burst candidates, presents side-by-side keep decisions, and exports a move-to-review-folder manifest. Non-goals: cloud photo hosting, face recognition, or automatic deletion.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot libraries complete review of 500+ assets and move 10%+ of candidates without a reported false-positive deletion in 30 days.
monetization: one-time — archive cleanup is episodic and users should not pay a subscription to expose private photos.
constraints: Local-only thumbnails and hashes; never alter originals; make moves explicit and reversible; perceptual hashing must be explained as a suggestion, not identity proof.
why_distinct: The product is a cautious decision workflow between detection and deletion, rather than another photo library or automatic deduper.

title: Restore Drill
user: Individuals and small teams backing up cloud files who need evidence that a local copy is restorable, not merely synchronized.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a cheap physical copy of cloud-synced files in case a provider terminates service; replies stress that synchronization is not backup.
An rclone backend advertises MD5 support but returns no MD5 for uploaded files, so an integration test cannot verify corrupted streamed uploads.

recurrence: The two sources independently show the same failure mode: a copy exists, but its completeness or integrity cannot be confidently demonstrated until recovery is needed.
current_workaround: Schedule rclone/restic jobs, glance at logs, or manually open a few files; few people retain a repeatable recovery record.
incumbents_and_gap: rclone, restic, NAS vendor sync tools, and cloud drives move bytes well. They do not give non-specialists a portable restore drill that samples content, records hash capability, and produces a plain-language recovery report.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that consumes a backup manifest, chooses deterministic sample files, verifies metadata/content where possible, guides a restore into a temporary directory, and writes a signed HTML/JSON drill report. Non-goals: performing backups, storing credentials, or replacing backup engines.
success_measure: At least 50% of installed users complete a second drill within 90 days, with each report containing a successful sampled restore or a clear failure cause.
monetization: free — trust and broad compatibility matter more than a hosted account; a paid team policy pack can follow only if demand appears.
constraints: Do not retain credentials; avoid writing into source directories; support providers without hashes honestly; temporary restored data must have a configurable cleanup path.
why_distinct: It verifies recovery readiness across existing tools instead of becoming another backup destination or sync client.

title: Confidential File Handoff
user: People sending tax, medical, legal, or credential files to non-technical recipients who need a simple, truthful, one-time handoff procedure.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker cannot make PGP, Signal installation, email attachments, and random sharing sites work for accountants, parents, and clients with sensitive documents.
A LocalSend issue challenges an end-to-end-encryption claim, distinguishing TLS transport encryption from true E2EE and showing users need precise security communication.

recurrence: Independent threads show both usability and security-language failure: recipient friction pushes people to unsafe channels, while misleading labels undermine informed choice.
current_workaround: Email attachments, Google Drive, a password in a second channel, Signal, Bitwarden Send, or improvised password-protected archives.
incumbents_and_gap: Bitwarden Send, Signal, OnionShare, LocalSend, and cloud drives move files, but users still have to decide a method and explain access, expiry, password delivery, and revocation to a recipient.
smallest_useful_product: A local wizard that creates an encrypted ZIP, generates a recipient-specific plain-language handoff sheet and two-channel password instructions, and tracks a manual acknowledgement checklist. Non-goals: hosting files, claiming E2EE where it is absent, identity verification, or legal compliance certification.
success_measure: In usability tests, 8 of 10 non-technical recipients retrieve and open a test document without sender support while correctly identifying where the password arrives.
monetization: one-time — valuable during occasional high-stakes exchanges, with no reason to retain customer documents.
constraints: Use audited browser cryptography or a native helper; do not log filenames/passwords; state threat model plainly; no medical/legal security guarantees.
why_distinct: It improves the human handoff and truthful threat-model communication around existing transfer methods rather than operating a new file-sharing service.

title: RSS Saved Queue
user: RSS-reader users who want saved web articles to re-enter their existing reading workflow as a private feed instead of accumulating in a separate read-later silo.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A long-time Instapaper user explicitly asks for a service that turns saved articles into a unique RSS feed usable in their feed reader.
Wallabag users request native Atom/RSS ingestion because they otherwise must save feed items one-by-one or rely on external automation.

recurrence: Two independent read-later communities describe the seam between feeds and saved articles; both currently need manual saving or auxiliary tooling.
current_workaround: Use a separate Instapaper/Pocket-like inbox, public Raindrop feeds, automation services, or manually copy URLs into a reader.
incumbents_and_gap: Instapaper, Wallabag, Raindrop, Readwise Reader, and RSS readers cover parts of the workflow; few offer a small private, standards-based bridge with a reviewable queue and no broader knowledge-management suite.
smallest_useful_product: A self-hostable service plus browser extension that saves URL/title/tags, serves an authenticated per-user RSS/Atom queue, and marks items read via the extension or feed-reader token endpoint. Non-goals: article scraping bypass, social feed aggregation, recommendation algorithms, or AI summaries.
success_measure: At least 40% of early users add the feed to a reader and process 20 saved items through it within 30 days.
monetization: freemium — a small hosted private feed is convenient, while self-hosting preserves an independent free path.
constraints: Private tokens must be revocable and non-guessable; respect publisher access and robots rules; retain only user-supplied metadata unless extraction is explicitly enabled.
why_distinct: It is an interoperability bridge between save actions and RSS habits, not a replacement feed reader or generic bookmark app.

title: Receipt Statement Linker
user: Freelancers and households who make purchases online and need a privacy-preserving way to connect browser receipts with later bank or accounting-statement rows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An HN user proposes an encrypted browser extension that detects checkout pages to track expenses and subscriptions, indicating a need for purchase-time capture.
A Firefly III importer report says tags are missing from imported withdrawals, showing that transaction context is easily lost during financial-data handoff.

recurrence: The paired requests cover both ends of the same workflow: useful merchant context exists at checkout but fails to survive into imported transactions.
current_workaround: Search email receipts, attach screenshots manually, guess from abbreviated merchant names, or trust opaque bank categorization.
incumbents_and_gap: Firefly III, Actual, Monarch, and receipt OCR tools track transactions, but a small local tool that stores a user-owned receipt-to-statement matching sidecar is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first browser extension that lets users save a receipt URL/merchant/amount/date at checkout, then matches an imported CSV by amount/date/merchant and exports a reviewable enriched CSV plus attachment manifest. Non-goals: bank credential aggregation, automatic spending advice, receipt OCR, or tax filing.
success_measure: At least 70% of a user's captured purchases are matched to a statement row with user approval, and fewer than 2% of approved matches are later corrected.
monetization: one-time — the extension handles private data locally and solves a focused recurring chore without a hosted account.
constraints: No bank login access; process statement files locally; provide false-match review; do not claim accounting or tax correctness; minimize page permissions.
why_distinct: It preserves purchase provenance across a handoff boundary rather than becoming another budgeting dashboard or checkout scraper.

title: Accessible Table OCR Check
user: Readers, librarians, and accessibility practitioners converting scanned tables who need to verify that extracted text retains reading order and cell structure before sharing it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A reader asks how to turn scanned-book PDFs into usable text for audiobooks and personal notes after classic OCR mangles words.
A user reports that OCR of a scanned table is read line-by-line rather than as cells, creating screen-reader accessibility problems.

recurrence: Both 2025 requests need more than an OCR text dump: one needs trustworthy text for listening/copying and the other needs table structure that assistive technology can follow.
current_workaround: Try several OCR engines, manually retype tables, or accept an unstructured PDF/text layer and discover errors only while reading it.
incumbents_and_gap: OCRmyPDF, Tesseract, Adobe Acrobat, and cloud OCR produce text, but they do not provide a lightweight visual-versus-reading-order review focused on tables and an accessible correction export.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA that accepts page images/OCR JSON, overlays detected blocks and reading order, lets a user relabel table cells and headers, and exports HTML/CSV plus an issue report. Non-goals: training an OCR model, hosting copyrighted books, full document editing, or automatic perfect reconstruction.
success_measure: In tests on 30 scanned table pages, reviewers can identify every deliberately scrambled reading-order defect and export an accessible table in under five minutes per page.
monetization: one-time — it is a specialized local verification aid for occasional batches.
constraints: Local processing by default; clarify that copyright permissions remain the user's responsibility; exports must use semantic HTML table headers and retain source-page references.
why_distinct: It is a human QA layer for OCR accessibility, not an LLM OCR wrapper or a generic PDF editor.

title: Tab Sunset List
user: Knowledge workers with chronic browser-tab overload who need a low-friction way to turn stale tabs into deliberate keep, schedule, bookmark, or close decisions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks directly how people handle browser tab overload; responses include closing tabs or using specialized tools.
Firefox iOS is asked to expose tab groups arriving from synced desktop devices, showing that even native tab grouping does not resolve cross-device tab accumulation.

recurrence: A direct user question and an independent browser feature request in the same month show that unmanaged tabs remain a cross-device utility problem.
current_workaround: Keep everything open, bulk-close tabs, create tab groups, or move important pages into bookmarks/read-later services.
incumbents_and_gap: Native tab groups, OneTab, Workona, and session managers store tabs; the unresolved gap is a deliberate expiry queue that asks for a decision after a chosen age and preserves a compact rationale.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that tags tabs with an expiry date and decision type, presents a daily small review queue, and exports kept items to browser bookmarks or Markdown. Non-goals: a new browser, cloud sync, AI summaries, or replacing native session restore.
success_measure: Among weekly active pilots, median open-tab count falls 30% after four weeks while at least 80% of explicitly saved tabs remain retrievable.
monetization: free — the minimal browser utility gains trust without a cloud account; optional one-time cross-browser export could follow.
constraints: Use only tabs/bookmarks permissions needed; never send browsing history off device; make close actions undoable while browser APIs allow it.
why_distinct: It uses time-bounded decisions and exportable outcomes, rather than treating tab hoarding as a storage or workspace-management problem.

title: Timezone Slot Proof
user: Solo professionals publishing booking links who need proof that their stated working hours produce the intended slots across invitee time zones and DST boundaries.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo-focused Ask HN thread seeks the essential capabilities of a simple one-to-one calendar scheduling tool rather than another feature-heavy scheduler.
A Cal.com issue documents afternoon availability shifting one hour late on a DST transition date, offering bookers an hour outside configured working time.

recurrence: The scheduling-market request and a concrete DST availability defect point to a basic but costly trust gap: owners cannot easily inspect what invitees will see.
current_workaround: Create test bookings, manually reason about time zones, or discover wrong slots after a client books them.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly, Cal.com, and SavvyCal schedule meetings, but their configuration UIs do not offer a portable, scenario-based proof of slots around daylight-saving transitions and multiple invitee zones.
smallest_useful_product: A static web tool that imports an ICS availability window or accepts weekly hours, renders the next 18 months of slots for selected zones, highlights DST discontinuities, and exports a shareable test matrix. Non-goals: accepting bookings, calendar OAuth, or acting as a scheduling service.
success_measure: For a seeded DST test suite, the tool flags 100% of intentionally shifted/missing slots and users can complete a five-zone review in under three minutes.
monetization: free — a public, deterministic validator benefits from easy access; paid team policy templates are only a later option.
constraints: Use current IANA timezone data; label results as a configuration check rather than a guarantee of third-party scheduler behavior; avoid calendar credentials.
why_distinct: It validates scheduling outputs without competing as another booking calendar.

title: Photo Exit Manifest
user: Families leaving Google Photos or another consumer cloud who need a verifiable, interruption-safe migration plan into an independent archive without losing albums, edits, or device expectations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Pixel-owning parent asks how to de-Google photos after running out of storage and explicitly worries about lockout and preserving automatic backup.
An Immich feature request says one-way device-to-server sync leaves edits, deletes, and cross-device expectations unresolved and asks for explicit conflict policies.

recurrence: The sources show that migration is not merely copying bytes: families need to account for device behavior, edits, deletion semantics, and a safe fallback before changing providers.
current_workaround: Export Takeout, copy folders into a NAS/Immich, and manually compare counts; keep paying for the original service because they cannot prove the new setup is complete.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout, rclone, Immich, PhotoPrism, and NAS products move/store photos. They lack a provider-neutral exit manifest that inventories expected assets/metadata and makes sync/deletion policies explicit before cutover.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that reads export inventories and destination folder reports, compares counts/hashes/dates/albums where available, records desired backup/mirror policies per device, and writes a cutover checklist with exceptions. Non-goals: transferring data, hosting photos, facial recognition, or two-way syncing.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot migrations end with a signed manifest accounting for 99.5%+ of source assets or a named exception for every difference.
monetization: one-time — migration assurance is a bounded, high-trust task and should not require retaining family archives.
constraints: Run entirely locally; support Takeout's changing formats defensively; never modify source/destination; clarify that proprietary edits may be non-portable.
why_distinct: It is a migration assurance layer across providers, not a replacement photo cloud or sync engine.

title: Payout Reconciliation Explainer
user: Small ecommerce operators and their bookkeepers who need to reconcile processor payouts against orders, refunds, fees, and bank deposits without opaque enterprise accounting tooling.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An ecommerce reconciliation builder asks businesses and accountants what is most frustrating about matching Shopify, payment-provider, and accounting numbers and explaining mismatches.
An Actual Budget user asks for a reconciliation workflow that infers principal versus interest from balances because imported payment data lacks the necessary split.

recurrence: Both 2026 requests center on incomplete financial exports: totals are available but the explanation for a difference is not, creating repeated manual reconciliation work.
current_workaround: Export CSVs from Shopify/Stripe/bank systems, combine them in spreadsheets, and leave a manual memo trail for an accountant.
incumbents_and_gap: A2X, Link My Books, QuickBooks, Xero, and enterprise reconciliation systems automate accounting at a cost. A focused local explainer for one payout batch and its evidence trail is underserved.
smallest_useful_product: An offline web app that imports three CSVs (orders/events, payout, bank), applies transparent matching rules, shows fees/refunds/timing differences as a waterfall, and exports a reconciler CSV plus accountant handoff PDF. Non-goals: direct bank/Shopify connections, bookkeeping ledger, tax advice, or auto-posting journal entries.
success_measure: On a labelled pilot dataset, users explain at least 95% of payout-to-bank variance and produce a handoff package in under 20 minutes per payout period.
monetization: one-time — CSV-based reconciliation is a concrete utility that should not require uploading financial records or a recurring integration fee.
constraints: All financial data stays local; require user-mapped columns and visible rules; no accounting/tax claims; retain currency/date precision and audit trail.
why_distinct: It explains and hands off a single reconciliation rather than trying to replace accounting software or hide matching logic behind automation.

title: CSV Import Contract
user: Implementation consultants and operations staff preparing legacy CSV/XLSX exports for a system migration who need a repeatable, reviewable import contract rather than one-off spreadsheet cleanup.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A software implementer says cleaning and mapping legacy CSV/XLSX customer exports for import is always painful; a commenter independently describes the same financial-data work.
A csvkit user asks for visibility into detected delimiter, quote, escape, newline, and related syntax because automatic detection is otherwise opaque.

recurrence: Two 2025 sources show a common handoff failure: users must clean/mapping files and cannot inspect the parsing assumptions that determine whether an import is safe.
current_workaround: Open files in Excel, use regex/find-replace, test ten rows in the target system, and keep undocumented per-client cleanup steps.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel, OpenRefine, csvkit, Frictionless, and ETL tools transform data, but a small local utility that turns profiling decisions into a signed, reusable client-facing import contract is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A local PWA that profiles CSV/XLSX parsing, proposes a column map and deterministic validations, lets users define transformations, and exports a JSON contract, cleaned preview, and human-readable handoff report. Non-goals: cloud ETL, database connectors, LLM data repair, or executing production imports.
success_measure: In migration pilots, 75% of files pass a second independent import using the exported contract without a new manual cleanup step.
monetization: one-time — consultants can use it on sensitive client exports without subscription or data upload friction.
constraints: Files stay local; transformations must be deterministic and versioned; warn on destructive coercions; preserve original row numbers and values in error reports.
why_distinct: It creates a portable agreement about parsing and mapping, rather than simply being another spreadsheet or generic data-cleaning interface.
